question: Why can a flat-plane V8 generally use a lighter crankshaft?
options: Its crank pins are arranged in one plane, reducing counterweight requirements
It fires only once every 180 degrees
explanation: The simpler 180° crank arrangement can require less counterweight mass, helping reduce rotating inertia. Engine design still determines the final crankshaft mass.

question: Why do flat-plane V8s rev higher?
options: They have a lighter crankshaft and lower rotational inertia
They always use shorter connecting rods
explanation: A lighter rotating assembly can reduce rotational inertia. That can support faster acceleration of engine speed; the actual limit also depends on the complete engine design.

question: What is the key exhaust-pulse difference between these layouts?
options: A flat-plane V8 has no exhaust pulses
Both have globally uneven firing intervals
Flat-plane firing alternates banks, while cross-plane firing does not
Cross-plane V8s fire only from one bank
explanation: Every four-stroke V8 still has one firing event every 90° of crank rotation. The important difference here is how those events alternate between the two cylinder banks.
